The BusGuard-1k assurance pack contains repeated-crash and IOMMU-storm traces, concurrent-recovery interference bounds, and verified 1 ms admission certificates. How should I describe this artifact?

Describe it as an assurance pack containing three kinds of material: traces for repeated crashes and IOMMU fault storms, bounds on interference during concurrent recovery, and verified certificates for 1 ms device admission. The traces document the named fault conditions; the bounds address recovery interference; and the certificates record verified admission claims.

The description does not give the numerical interference bounds, identify the devices covered by the certificates, or report particular values from the traces. Those details should not be inferred from the pack’s name or contents.
Are the repeated-crash traces and IOMMU-storm traces the same thing?

No. They cover separately named conditions. Repeated-crash traces concern crashes that recur, while IOMMU-storm traces concern IOMMU fault storms. The pack contains both; the artifact description does not say they were captured in the same run or that every trace includes both conditions.
Does the pack tell us how many crashes occurred or how many IOMMU faults made up a storm?

Not in the stated description. It identifies repeated-crash and IOMMU-storm traces but gives no crash count, fault count, rate, or duration. Those could be properties of particular traces, but they are not values supplied here.
What do the concurrent-recovery interference bounds add beyond having traces?

They state bounded interference for concurrent recovery, whereas traces record behavior in the conditions they cover. A trace alone should not be treated as a general interference bound, and a bound alone does not describe every event in a trace.

The pack includes both forms of assurance material. Its description does not supply the bounds’ numerical values or their derivation, so it is best to name their subject—concurrent-recovery interference—without assigning them an unstated magnitude.
Can I say the concurrent-recovery interference bound is 0.09 ms?

Not solely from this artifact description. It says the pack contains concurrent-recovery interference bounds, but it does not state their values. If a particular bound in the pack is to be quoted, it should be identified by its actual stated value and scope rather than assumed from the pack’s title or from another result.
Does “bounds” mean there must be a different number for each admitted device?

No such breakdown is specified. The plural indicates that the pack contains interference bounds, but it does not say whether they differ by device, recovery condition, or another dimension. We should not invent a structure for them from the plural alone.
What can we say confidently about the admission certificates?

They are verified 1 ms admission certificates. That is a substantive property of the artifact: it contains verified certificates for admission against a 1 ms deadline. The description does not list the certified devices or groups, state how many certificates there are, or spell out every condition each certificate covers.

Accordingly, report the verified certificates as included, but do not turn their existence into a claim that every device or configuration has been admitted.
Is it too cautious to call them verified? The artifact explicitly says that.

No. “Verified” belongs in the description because it is explicitly stated. The caution is about scope, not about weakening that status. You can say the pack contains verified 1 ms admission certificates while leaving their individual subjects and conditions unspecified.
Could I say the certificates guarantee that any device meets a 1 ms deadline through any recovery?

No. A verified admission certificate supports the admission claim it covers; the artifact description does not say that it covers any device or every conceivable recovery condition. The pack’s stated subject includes concurrent recovery, but its description gives no universal coverage claim. Keep the 1 ms figure and the verification status without adding an unlimited guarantee.
Are the certificates for the faulting device as well as unaffected devices?

The hard-real-time admission concern here is the 1 ms service deadline for unaffected devices during faults and recovery. The artifact does not state that a device whose own driver has crashed receives a 1 ms guarantee while it restarts. It also does not identify the subjects of individual certificates, so avoid assigning one to the faulting device.
Does an admission certificate say recovery must finish within 1 ms?

No. The 1 ms value is a service deadline for devices admitted under that requirement, not a stated completion deadline for recovery. Concurrent recovery interference bounds matter because recovery can continue while an admitted device needs timely service.
Can the traces be presented as proving that no DMA ever escaped an IOMMU domain?

That would exceed the artifact description. It says the pack contains repeated-crash and IOMMU-storm traces, not that those traces show zero DMA escapes or prove a universal isolation property. The interference bounds and admission certificates address timing assurance; they should not be recast as an unstated DMA-isolation finding.
Does an IOMMU fault-storm trace itself show that an unaffected device missed its deadline?

The description gives no such trace outcome. An IOMMU-storm trace identifies material associated with that condition, but it does not tell us whether a deadline was met or missed in the trace. Nor should the presence of a fault storm be treated as proof of a memory escape.
Then what is the relationship between the traces, the bounds, and the certificates?

They are complementary contents of one assurance pack. The traces concern repeated crashes and IOMMU fault storms; the bounds concern interference from concurrent recovery; and the verified certificates concern 1 ms admission. Together they make the pack relevant to service during fault and recovery conditions.

The description does not specify a one-to-one mapping from a particular trace to a particular bound or certificate, or give the reasoning used to verify each certificate. Those links should not be invented when summarizing the pack.
Would it be fair to call the pack a completed implementation of BusGuard-1k?

Call it an assurance pack, as stated. It contains traces, interference bounds, and admission certificates; the description does not say it implements a DMA cap, scheduler, restart sequence, or other runtime control. Assurance material and an implementation are different kinds of artifacts.
What does the name BusGuard-1k contribute? Is “1k” a count of certificates?

BusGuard-1k is the pack’s name. The description provides no count of certificates, traces, crashes, or faults. The “1k” should not be interpreted as one thousand of any of those items; the timing value expressly stated for the certificates is 1 ms.
Could I describe the pack as covering concurrent recovery without claiming it covers every possible overlap?

Yes. Say it contains concurrent-recovery interference bounds. That directly names the covered subject without asserting that every possible pattern of concurrent recovery falls within those bounds. Any more specific coverage claim would need the bounds’ stated conditions.
Does the pack establish the 1 ms admission requirement in some sense, or is it merely a collection of proposed checks?

It is more than a proposal: the artifact contains *verified* 1 ms admission certificates. You can report that verified assurance material exists. At the same time, the description does not identify which admissions were certified or provide a universal conclusion for all devices. The appropriate claim is about the certificates the pack contains, at their stated 1 ms threshold.
If someone wants to quote a particular interference allowance, what can I tell them from this description?

Only that concurrent-recovery interference bounds are included. No numerical allowance appears in this artifact description, so a particular value cannot be quoted from it. They would need the relevant bound and its scope within the pack before using it in a device’s admission argument.
Should the report say that all three kinds of material concern exactly the same run?

No. The description says they are included in the same assurance pack, not that they were all produced in one run. It does not specify how the traces, bounds, and certificates are grouped internally or when each was produced. Listing the contents is accurate without inventing a shared-run claim.
What is a concise caption that preserves the verification claim and avoids adding results?

“The BusGuard-1k assurance pack contains repeated-crash and IOMMU-storm traces, concurrent-recovery interference bounds, and verified 1 ms admission certificates.” That reports the artifact’s contents and the certificates’ verification status without inventing trace outcomes, bound values, or universal coverage.

For bounded recovery, I propose per-device fault supervisors, generation-tagged IPC, preallocated restart images, and rate-limited interrupt remapping. How do these fit into a restartable device-driver isolation boundary?

They address different parts of a fault-and-restart transition. Per-device fault supervisors give each device a corresponding point of fault supervision. Generation-tagged IPC distinguishes communication associated with different driver instances. Preallocated restart images provide restart material without making its preparation part of fault-time recovery. Rate-limited interrupt remapping constrains interrupt delivery when a device generates excessive interrupts.

Together, they form a proposal for bounded recovery. They do not, merely by being named, establish a numerical recovery bound, contain every kind of DMA activity, or verify unaffected devices’ 1 ms service deadlines.
What does “per-device” contribute to the fault supervisors?

It makes supervision device-specific rather than describing one undifferentiated recovery operation for all devices. That matters when asking whether a fault associated with one driver can be handled without making unrelated devices participate in its recovery.

The proposal does not specify a supervisor’s internal design, how it detects a fault, or what actions it takes. Per-device supervision is the proposed structure, not a completed demonstration of independent recovery.
Can I say each supervisor guarantees that its device restarts successfully?

No. A fault supervisor is a proposed component for managing the device’s fault and restart boundary. The proposal does not state a restart-success rate, a completion deadline, or a guarantee that every fault is recoverable. “For bounded recovery” states the intended purpose of the combination, not an observed outcome for each supervisor.
Is a per-device supervisor the same as putting each driver in a separate address space?

They concern different things. An address space constrains where driver code can access memory. A fault supervisor concerns how a device-associated fault is managed across the transition into recovery and restart. One does not automatically provide the other.

This proposal specifies per-device fault supervisors; it does not replace the broader need to contain driver writes and device DMA.
Why tag IPC with a generation?

A restart creates a distinction between communication belonging to the previous driver instance and communication belonging to the new one. A generation tag makes that distinction explicit in IPC, so the recovery design can reason about whether a message is associated with the current instance rather than treating all pending messages as interchangeable.

The proposal does not specify a tag format, a generation-number width, or a particular rule for accepting and discarding messages.
Does generation-tagged IPC mean all old messages are automatically removed at restart?

No. Tagging provides information with which to distinguish generations; it is not, by itself, a claim that old messages have been removed or that a particular recipient ignores them. To establish a restart property, the design would need a rule for using the tags. That rule is not supplied in this proposal.
Is the tag applied to DMA transactions and interrupts too?

The proposal specifically says *generation-tagged IPC*. It should not be expanded into a claim that DMA transactions or interrupts carry those tags. DMA containment and interrupt control require their own account; rate-limited interrupt remapping is the interrupt-related element named here.

Generation tags address the identity of interprocess communication across driver instances, not every form of device activity.
Could a message from a failed driver arrive while the replacement driver is starting?

That is the sort of transition generation-tagged IPC is intended to make distinguishable: communication associated with one driver instance need not be mistaken for communication associated with another. The proposal does not report that such a message has arrived, specify queue behavior, or say how an individual message would be handled. It identifies a concern the design can address.
What are preallocated restart images meant to accomplish?

They make the material needed to start a driver available in advance, rather than requiring its preparation to be performed entirely as part of fault-time recovery. That can help make recovery work more predictable. It does not establish how quickly the driver starts or whether other recovery work is bounded.

The proposal gives no image size, storage arrangement, or preparation procedure.
Can I say preallocation makes restart instantaneous?

No. Having a restart image prepared does not eliminate the work of managing the fault and starting a new driver instance. “Preallocated” describes the state of the image before restart; it is not a zero-time restart claim or a measured upper bound.
Does the restart image include a known-good state for the device?

The proposal does not specify the contents of a restart image or assert that it represents a known-good device state. Calling it preallocated says the image is made available ahead of recovery. A claim about device state, image validation, or how it interacts with device reset would need additional information.
What is the role of rate-limited interrupt remapping?

It combines interrupt routing with a limit on delivery, so fault-associated interrupt activity cannot be treated as an unlimited demand on interrupt-handling service. In a bounded-recovery proposal, that is particularly relevant when an interrupt storm might coexist with restart work and with service for unaffected devices.

No rate, remapping configuration, or measured effect on service is specified here. The control’s presence is a proposal, not a verified storm-containment result.
Would remapping alone handle an interrupt storm?

Remapping identifies how interrupts are directed; the *rate-limited* qualification is what addresses an excessive rate. Neither term alone proves that the system can process or constrain every pending interrupt under a particular fault. The proposal names both properties together but does not define their limits or the behavior of already queued interrupts.
If interrupts are rate-limited, may I assume they consume none of an unaffected device’s reserved service?

No. A limit need not mean zero interrupt work. To protect unaffected devices’ service, the remaining interrupt demand and any recovery work would need to fit within an appropriate timing argument. This proposal gives no interrupt-rate value or service accounting from which to conclude that reserved slots are untouched.
Do the four mechanisms all act at the same point in restart?

Not necessarily. They describe different aspects of the transition: supervision of a device-associated fault, identification of IPC across driver instances, availability of restart material, and constrained interrupt delivery. The proposal does not set an operational sequence among them, so their listing should not be read as a prescribed order.
Could you explain the division between containing an old driver instance and starting the new one?

Generation-tagged IPC is relevant to distinguishing old-instance communication from new-instance communication. Rate-limited interrupt remapping is relevant to constraining interrupt pressure while that distinction matters. Per-device fault supervisors and preallocated restart images concern organizing recovery and making a new instance available.

Those roles are conceptual. The proposal does not specify a point at which the old instance is fully contained or the new one may begin, so we should not assert a completed handoff procedure.
When you say “bounded recovery,” is the bound 1 ms?

No such recovery-duration bound is stated. The 1 ms figure in the overall goal is a service deadline for unaffected devices while driver faults and recovery occur. Bounded recovery here means the proposed mechanisms are intended to make recovery’s behavior and interference subject to limits; it does not say the restarting driver must finish recovery within 1 ms.
Could recovery be bounded yet still disrupt that 1 ms service deadline?

Conceptually, yes. An upper bound on recovery work could still be too large, or could fall at the wrong time, for an unaffected device’s deadline. The recovery bound would have to be composed with the service and other interference that matter to the 1 ms requirement.

This proposal gives neither a numerical recovery bound nor a verification result, so compatibility with the deadline remains to be established.
Does this proposal, by itself, fence stale DMA from a failed driver’s device?

No. None of its four named elements, simply by being listed, establishes a DMA fence. Generation-tagged IPC concerns messages; rate-limited interrupt remapping concerns interrupts; supervisors and restart images concern recovery organization. The overall isolation boundary still has to contain device-initiated DMA across crashes and restarts, but this proposal does not specify a new DMA-fencing sequence.
Does “per-device” supervision make a device independently isolated from every other device?

No. Supervision granularity is not the same as independent hardware isolation. A device may have its own fault supervisor without that fact alone establishing its DMA routing, IOMMU-group isolation, or bus-service behavior. The proposal concerns bounded recovery and should not be presented as a complete hardware-isolation proof.
Can generation tags substitute for isolating arbitrary driver memory writes?

No. Tags help distinguish IPC associated with different driver generations; they do not constrain where driver code may write memory. A driver could misuse memory independently of the IPC it sends. The two concerns require distinct arguments.
Why combine a prepared image with a supervisor rather than treating them as one feature?

They serve different conceptual roles. The supervisor provides a device-specific locus for managing faults and restarts; the preallocated image provides material for launching a replacement instance. Naming both avoids treating the decision to restart as though it automatically makes the restart material available, or treating prepared material as though it decides when recovery should occur.

No interface between them is specified in the proposal.
What does the proposal say about repeated crashes during recovery?

It does not give a repeated-crash policy or a bound for multiple recovery episodes. Per-device supervision and generation-tagged IPC are relevant concepts when driver instances change, but the proposal does not state how many changes are supported in a given interval or how a further fault would be handled. That remains outside its explicit detail.
Could a new generation reuse a tag while old communication is still pending?

That is a valid general question for the design of generation-tagged IPC, but this proposal specifies no tag space or reuse rule. We cannot claim that reuse is safe, unsafe, or handled by a particular mechanism here. The faithful point is that tags are proposed to distinguish driver generations; the conditions under which that distinction remains unambiguous would need to be established.
What should a timing argument for this proposal account for?

It would need to account for fault-supervision work, restart work using the preallocated images, and interrupt activity under the rate-limited remapping policy insofar as they can interfere with service for unaffected devices. It would also have to consider the relevant overlap between those activities and the unaffected devices’ 1 ms deadline intervals.

That is an outline of what the proposed bounded-recovery claim would require, not a specified budget, measured cost, or completed verification.
Does the proposal set a limit for the interrupt rate or say how much CPU time supervision gets?

No. It specifies *rate-limited* interrupt remapping but no numerical rate. It specifies *per-device* fault supervisors but no CPU allocation or execution-time bound. Those values cannot be invented from the mechanism names; their adequacy for bounded recovery and unaffected-device service would need to be shown separately.
If the images are preallocated, should I assume they consume no memory-bus service during recovery?

No. Preallocation says something about availability before recovery, not that starting from an image uses no resources. A timing argument must account for any recovery activity that can affect deadline-relevant CPU or bus service. The proposal supplies no measurement or rule that makes image use free of interference.
How do I describe what is being bounded without promising that the fault itself ends quickly?

Distinguish bounded handling and interference from a promise that every fault resolves immediately. The proposed supervisors, generation tags, prepared images, and limited interrupt delivery are intended to make the transition through fault handling and restart more predictable and containable. The proposal does not supply a time to fault resolution or guarantee that the affected device returns to service by a particular deadline.
Would it be accurate to call this a replacement for the DMA and deadline admission controls?

No. It is an additional bounded-recovery proposal. It does not eliminate the need to contain arbitrary writes and DMA or to establish unaffected devices’ 1 ms service deadlines during faults and concurrent recovery. Recovery organization, memory isolation, and deadline admission are complementary concerns, not interchangeable labels for one control.
What claims must remain open even if all four features appear in an implementation?

Their implementation would not by itself establish a worst-case recovery duration, demonstrate that stale IPC cannot be misapplied, show the disposition of queued interrupts, prove DMA containment, or verify the 1 ms service deadlines for unaffected devices. Each of those claims needs an argument or evidence at its own scope.

The current node is a proposal for four features and bounded recovery, not a report of their implementation or validation.
Give me a concise version that names every component and preserves its status as a proposal.

Propose per-device fault supervisors, generation-tagged IPC, preallocated restart images, and rate-limited interrupt remapping to support bounded driver recovery. The proposal defines a recovery structure; it does not yet establish a numerical recovery bound, DMA containment, or verified 1 ms service deadlines for unaffected devices.
How are queued completions and MSI-X interrupts from a crashed driver rejected after its replacement starts?

That is an open handoff question. Starting a replacement driver does not, by itself, establish that pending activity belongs to the replacement. The boundary needs a way to distinguish activity associated with the crashed instance from activity the new instance is allowed to accept, and it needs to maintain that distinction even when delivery occurs after the replacement starts.

Queued completions and MSI-X interrupts need separate accounts. Generation-tagged IPC could help distinguish driver generations for communication covered by IPC, while rate-limited interrupt remapping concerns interrupt delivery. Neither proposal alone specifies how a queued completion or an already pending MSI-X interrupt is rejected.
What do you mean by rejecting a queued completion?

The relevant property is that a completion associated with the crashed instance must not be treated as a valid completion of the replacement instance’s work. It might still exist or arrive after the replacement starts; the question is how the boundary prevents that late arrival from being accepted as current.

The node does not specify the completion queue, its producer, or a particular rejection rule. So we can state the required distinction without claiming that old completions have already been discarded.
Wouldn't generation-tagged IPC handle the completions?

It could contribute if the queued completions reach the replacement through IPC whose generation is checked. But the proposal only says that IPC is generation-tagged. It does not say that every queued completion carries such a tag, that every recipient checks it, or what happens when a tag identifies the crashed instance.

An answer would have to establish those links rather than infer them from the presence of generation tags.
So a tag on a message isn't the same as a rejection policy?

Exactly. A tag can identify which driver generation a message belongs to. Rejection requires a rule that uses that identity when deciding whether the replacement may act on the message. The question asks for the latter property as well as the ability to distinguish generations.

It also asks about MSI-X interrupts, which should not be assumed to carry an IPC generation tag.
Why single out MSI-X interrupts rather than just saying interrupts?

It makes the pending-interrupt part of the question specific. The boundary must account for MSI-X interrupts associated with the crashed driver that remain queued when its replacement starts. A general promise to limit interrupt rates would not, on its own, say whether those particular pending interrupts are rejected as old activity.

Nothing here specifies an MSI-X configuration, a queue depth, or how many interrupts are pending.
Does rate-limited interrupt remapping solve that identification problem?

Rate limiting addresses how much interrupt delivery can occur; remapping concerns where interrupts are delivered. Those properties are relevant to containing an interrupt storm, but neither automatically identifies whether a pending interrupt belongs to the crashed instance or the replacement.

The question therefore remains open even with rate-limited interrupt remapping in the proposal: what prevents an old MSI-X interrupt from being interpreted as an event for the new driver?
Could we just ignore all interrupts until the replacement is running?

That description leaves out the critical boundary. If an interrupt is already queued, delaying its handling until the replacement runs could present old activity to the new instance. Conversely, saying interrupts are ignored does not specify when delivery resumes or how pending events are distinguished.

The question is not merely whether delivery pauses. It is how old MSI-X interrupts are rejected *after* the replacement starts, without inadvertently accepting them as current.
Is the same issue present if we simply clear a completion queue during restart?

Clearing a queue would address entries present at the moment it is cleared, but the question also concerns what happens if activity from the crashed instance is still pending or becomes visible after that point. A queue-clear operation, by its name alone, does not establish that no old completion can arrive later or be accepted.

That is a conceptual distinction, not a claim that a particular queue is cleared in this design.
What boundary has to exist between the old and new instances?

There has to be an unambiguous acceptance boundary: work attributable to the crashed driver remains old even if it is delivered after the replacement starts, while legitimately new work can be recognized as belonging to the replacement. The boundary has to apply to each relevant form of queued completion and MSI-X interrupt, not just to the act of launching the new process.

The question supplies no concrete protocol for establishing that boundary, so the acceptance rule and its enforcement remain to be specified.
Can we say everything delivered after restart belongs to the new driver?

No. Delivery time is not the same as origin. The question expressly concerns completions and MSI-X interrupts *from a crashed driver* arriving or remaining queued after its replacement starts. Treating delivery after restart as proof of current ownership would assume away the stale-activity problem.
Could everything delivered before restart simply be considered old?

That may help identify some old activity, but it does not settle what was queued before restart and delivered afterward. The question focuses on that crossing of the handoff boundary. An answer needs to distinguish origin or validity, not just the time at which the replacement happens to observe an event.
Would a per-device fault supervisor be the place to make that distinction?

Per-device supervision provides a proposed point for managing a device-associated fault and restart. It could be part of an account of which driver instance is current, but the proposal does not specify that the supervisor examines completions, filters interrupts, or applies a particular acceptance rule.

Its existence is not itself evidence that stale events are rejected. The handoff behavior still needs to be defined.
What does “queued” add to the problem?

It means the event can outlast the driver instance with which it is associated. Even if further activity is constrained during recovery, a completion or MSI-X interrupt already pending could remain available for delivery when the replacement begins. That makes the restart boundary a question of pending work, not only of preventing new work from the crashed instance.

The question does not specify where either kind of event is queued or how long it remains there.
Can I treat a queued completion and a queued MSI-X interrupt as one stale message?

Only as a shorthand for the overall concern, not as a single mechanism. A completion and an MSI-X interrupt may travel through different paths and have different acceptance points. Generation-tagged IPC speaks directly to communication that uses that IPC; interrupt remapping and its rate limit speak to interrupt delivery. An answer must account for both kinds of old activity without assuming the same tag or rejection mechanism applies to each.
Does rejecting an interrupt necessarily mean no interrupt-handling work occurs at all?

No. The essential requirement is that an old interrupt not be accepted as a valid event for the replacement driver. Recognizing and rejecting it might itself require some handling. The question does not give a handling cost or say that rejection is instantaneous.

That distinction matters to the overall 1 ms requirement for unaffected devices: even a correct rejection rule would still need to coexist with timely service during recovery.
Could the replacement driver inspect an interrupt and decide whether it looks stale?

That is one possible kind of question for a concrete design, but “looks stale” is not yet an established criterion. To rely on such a decision, the design would have to identify information that reliably distinguishes the crashed instance’s event from the replacement’s event, including across the restart handoff.

The current question asks how rejection is achieved; it does not specify that the replacement driver performs the check or that it has enough information to do so.
Would preallocated restart images help reject these old events?

Preallocated restart images concern having restart material ready. They do not, by themselves, identify the generation of a queued completion or pending MSI-X interrupt. Starting a prepared replacement more quickly would not make an old event become new or specify how the event is rejected.
If IPC is generation-tagged, what exactly still needs to be shown for completions?

An answer would need to show that the completions in question are associated with a generation in a form the acceptance boundary can check, that the replacement uses the current generation when deciding what to accept, and that a completion from the crashed generation cannot be mistaken for current work. It would also need to account for any completion path not covered by the IPC tagging proposal.

Those are conditions an answer would have to establish, not implementation details reported as already present.
What similarly needs to be shown for the MSI-X side?

The design needs an account of MSI-X interrupts pending from the crashed instance: where they can be delivered during the handoff, how they are prevented from being accepted as events of the replacement, and what permits current interrupt delivery to proceed afterward. Rate-limited remapping can bound and direct delivery, but the disposition of already queued old interrupts must be addressed explicitly.

The node supplies no particular remapping rule or validation result for that disposition.
Does a reset automatically mark all pending completions and MSI-X interrupts as rejected?

That cannot be assumed from this question. Reset may be relevant to a restart boundary, but the question asks specifically how queued completions and MSI-X interrupts from a crashed driver are rejected after replacement starts. Without a stated account of pending events and their acceptance points, naming a reset would not answer it.
Is rejection about preventing a security escape, a timing overrun, or both?

The immediate issue is correctness of the restart boundary: old work must not be mistaken for new work. The broader design also requires fault containment and unaffected devices’ verified 1 ms service deadlines during faults and recovery. Handling a backlog of old interrupts could affect timing, but this question gives no timing bound or observed deadline result.

So the rejection rule and its cost both matter to the broader goal, without treating either as already established.
Could we claim the problem is solved if the replacement receives no stale IPC messages in one run?

That observation alone would not answer the whole question. It would not necessarily cover every queued completion path, nor would it establish what happens to pending MSI-X interrupts. The question asks for a boundary that rejects activity associated with the crashed driver after replacement begins, rather than merely an instance in which no such delivery was observed.
What would be a precise way to state the remaining question without deciding on a mechanism?

What acceptance and interrupt-delivery rules ensure that queued completions and MSI-X interrupts attributable to a crashed driver cannot be treated as valid events for its replacement after the replacement starts? That keeps both kinds of pending activity explicit while leaving open how generation-tagged IPC, supervision, and rate-limited interrupt remapping would be used to enforce the boundary.

I want to extend BusGuard-1k with delayed completions and MSI-X floods across 100 restarts, then verify generation checks, interrupt drainage, and the 1 ms certificates. How should I describe this activity?

Describe it as an extension to exercise pending work at the driver-replacement boundary. Introduce delayed completions and MSI-X floods across 100 restarts, then check that generation checks distinguish old work from work the replacement may accept, that interrupts are drained as required for the handoff, and that the 1 ms admission certificates are verified against the extended conditions.

Those are the activity and its checks, not findings. The node does not report that a delayed completion was rejected, that interrupt drainage completed, or that the certificates passed this verification.
Does “across 100 restarts” mean 100 delayed completions and 100 MSI-X floods?

No. The stated count is 100 restarts. It does not give a count of delayed completions or floods, or say that each condition is injected exactly once per restart. Keep the restart count explicit without assigning unstated counts to the injected events.
Why introduce delayed completions instead of checking only what is already in a completion queue when a driver crashes?

A delayed completion tests the handoff across time: work associated with the earlier driver instance may become visible after its replacement starts. Examining only entries present at one instant would not necessarily exercise that situation. The generation check needs to distinguish which instance a completion belongs to when acceptance is decided.

The activity does not specify a completion queue, a delivery delay, or how the delay is produced.
What is a generation check supposed to establish during this activity?

It is meant to establish that a completion attributable to the crashed driver is not accepted as valid work for the replacement merely because it arrives after the replacement has started. The check should distinguish the relevant driver generations at the point where the completion might be accepted.

The activity calls for verifying that behavior. It does not give a tag format, a rejection rule, or a result showing that the distinction holds.
Can I say every delayed completion in the test is necessarily from a crashed driver?

The activity names delayed completions in the context of testing the restart handoff, but it does not give a breakdown of their origins. Its generation checks should address the distinction between work belonging to the crashed instance and work belonging to its replacement. Do not assign an origin to every individual injected completion without a stated test procedure or result.
If the replacement happens to receive no old completions, would that verify generation checks?

Not on that observation alone. To verify a generation check, the activity needs to exercise or otherwise account for the decision that separates old-generation completions from current-generation work. Merely observing no old completion at the replacement would not show how one would be handled if it arrived.

That describes the purpose of the check, not a prescribed injection method or a reported outcome.
Why specify MSI-X floods separately from delayed completions?

They challenge different paths through the restart boundary. A delayed completion raises the question of whether old work is accepted as current work. An MSI-X flood raises questions about pending interrupt delivery and whether its drainage is completed without allowing old interrupts to be mistaken for replacement-driver events. It can also create service pressure while recovery is occurring.

A generation check for completions cannot, without further argument, stand in for verifying interrupt drainage.
Does “interrupt drainage” mean the MSI-X floods are stopped before each replacement starts?

The activity says to verify interrupt drainage; it does not specify an exact stopping point or an operational sequence. The relevant property is that pending interrupts associated with a crashed driver are accounted for at the handoff, so they are not silently treated as events of the replacement.

It would be premature to say that every flood stops before restart or that all pending interrupts have already been drained.
Would rate-limited interrupt remapping alone count as verified drainage?

No. A rate limit concerns how much interrupt delivery occurs; drainage concerns what happens to interrupts already pending around restart. The activity specifically calls for verifying drainage under MSI-X floods, so the existence of a delivery limit would not, by itself, supply that verification.
Does an interrupt have to carry an IPC generation tag for this activity to work?

That is not specified. Generation checks and interrupt drainage are separate checks in the activity; it does not say that an MSI-X interrupt carries an IPC tag or that the same mechanism handles both events. The verification needs to account for each path without inventing a shared representation.
What if an old MSI-X interrupt is recognized and discarded, but recognizing it takes some time?

Correct rejection and timing are separate questions. Handling an interrupt before discarding it could still require service, so the 1 ms certificate check matters alongside drainage. The activity does not give a handling cost or say whether any such work consumes service reserved for unaffected devices.

It calls for verifying both the handoff behavior and the 1 ms assurance under the extended conditions.
Is verifying the 1 ms certificates the same as checking that all 100 restarts complete within 1 ms?

No. The 1 ms figure concerns service for admitted, unaffected devices during faults and recovery, not the time required to complete a restart. The certificate verification should address that service deadline in the presence of the added delayed-completion and MSI-X-flood conditions. No restart-completion deadline is stated.
Does the existence of 1 ms admission certificates mean we can skip their verification in this extension?

No. Verifying the 1 ms certificates is expressly part of this activity. The extension adds delayed completions and MSI-X floods across restarts, and the check asks whether the certificate claims are justified for the conditions being examined. The activity does not state the outcome of that check.
Should I say this activity creates 100 new admission certificates?

No. One hundred counts restarts, not certificates. The activity says to verify 1 ms certificates; it does not specify how many certificates exist, whether any are newly issued, or a one-to-one relationship between restarts and certificates.
Could a certificate check pass even if an old completion is accepted by the replacement?

The checks should remain separate. A certificate concerns the 1 ms service-deadline assurance, while generation checks concern whether old completion work can be accepted as new. A timing result would not excuse a failed handoff check, and a successful handoff check would not automatically verify the deadline certificates.

No outcome for either check is reported here.
And could generation checks and drainage pass while an unaffected device misses 1 ms?

Conceptually, yes. Correctly rejecting old events does not necessarily make the work involved free of timing cost. That is why the activity also verifies the 1 ms certificates. It is intended to test both restart-boundary correctness and the service guarantee during the extended fault and recovery conditions, rather than infer one from the other.
Would checking service timing only after each replacement has settled be enough?

No. The deadline concern is service during faults and concurrent recovery. Delayed completions and MSI-X floods matter particularly around the handoff, so a check restricted to settled operation afterward would not cover the period this activity is extending BusGuard-1k to examine.
Can I claim the extension proves that every queued completion and MSI-X interrupt will be rejected in any future crash?

No. This node specifies an activity and no findings. Even after it is run, a result would need to be reported with the scope and conditions actually covered. The accurate present statement is that delayed completions and MSI-X floods will be exercised across 100 restarts to verify generation checks and interrupt drainage; it is not a universal rejection result.
Does it specify how many MSI-X vectors or how intense the floods are?

No. It names MSI-X floods but supplies no vector count, interrupt rate, flood duration, or distribution across the 100 restarts. Those details should not be inferred from the test name or the restart count.
What does the BusGuard-1k name contribute here? Is “1k” another numerical target?

It identifies the activity being extended. The explicit count for this extension is 100 restarts, and the explicit service deadline is 1 ms. The “1k” in BusGuard-1k does not establish a count of injections, interrupts, certificates, or restarts.
Should we also say this activity remeasures the 0.09 ms recovery-interference bound?

That is not stated. The activity calls for delayed-completion and MSI-X-flood injections across 100 restarts and verification of generation checks, interrupt drainage, and 1 ms certificates. It does not specify a new interference measurement or report a new numerical bound. The deadline verification should not be relabeled as a remeasurement of 0.09 ms.
Is this a peer-to-peer DMA or cross-domain-write test too?

Not as described. Its new injected conditions are delayed completions and MSI-X floods, and its named checks are generation checks, interrupt drainage, and 1 ms certificates. It should not be reported as producing a new peer-DMA, requester-ID, or cross-domain-write finding.
How do I keep the word “verify” from sounding as though all three checks have already passed?

Use it as the verb for work to be performed: *extend* BusGuard-1k with the named injections, then *verify* the three named properties. Do not say “verified generation checks” or “validated interrupt drainage” as results until findings are reported. The same applies to the certificates under this extended condition.
Can you give me one compact activity statement that preserves every number and condition?

Extend BusGuard-1k by injecting delayed completions and MSI-X floods across 100 restarts; verify generation checks, interrupt drainage, and the 1 ms admission certificates under those conditions. The activity states what will be exercised and checked, not the outcome of any check.

The BusGuard-1k extension reports that, across 100 restarts, generation checks rejected 12,000 stale completions; MSI-X remapping capped floods at 50/ms; and unaffected-device response was ≤0.96 ms. How should we report this evidence?

Keep the three findings distinct. Across 100 restarts, generation checks rejected 12,000 stale completions. MSI-X remapping capped floods at 50/ms. Unaffected-device response was ≤0.96 ms, below the 1 ms service deadline for the reported conditions.

The findings address stale-completion rejection, interrupt-flood limiting, and unaffected-device timing. They do not separately state an interrupt-drainage result or identify the contribution of each control to the response bound.
Does 12,000 mean that many stale completions were rejected on every restart?

No. It is the total number of stale completions reported as rejected across 100 restarts. The evidence gives no per-restart distribution. It would be inaccurate to turn the total into a count for each restart.
Can I calculate 120 rejected completions per restart?

You can calculate 12,000 divided by 100, which is 120 as an arithmetic average per restart. But that does not mean exactly 120 were rejected on each restart, and the evidence does not report that average as a measured per-restart result. The direct finding is 12,000 rejected across 100 restarts.
What did the generation checks establish about the replacement driver?

For the 12,000 stale completions reported, the generation checks rejected them rather than accepting them as current work. That is directly relevant to distinguishing work associated with an earlier driver instance from work the replacement may accept.

The result does not specify the representation of the generation, where the check occurred, or how many other completions were processed.
Can I say every stale completion that could ever arrive after restart will be rejected?

Not from this count alone. The evidence reports rejection of 12,000 stale completions across the 100 restarts. It does not state an exhaustive result for every possible completion or future restart. Report the observed scope without replacing it with a universal guarantee.
Does the result tell us how many delayed completions were injected in total?

It gives the number of stale completions rejected: 12,000. It does not separately give a total number of injected completions or a breakdown of completion types. Calling 12,000 the complete injection count would add a fact not stated.
What exactly does the 50/ms figure refer to?

It is the reported cap on MSI-X floods provided by MSI-X remapping: 50 per millisecond. It is a rate limit on the flood, not a 50 ms recovery duration, a count of 50 restarts, or a bound on unaffected-device response time.
Does a cap of 50/ms mean exactly 50 MSI-X interrupts arrived in every millisecond?

No. A cap is a limit, not a statement that delivery always reaches it. The evidence does not give an interrupt count for each millisecond or specify the exact measurement windows used to establish the reported 50/ms rate.
Can we say the MSI-X flood was eliminated?

No. The finding is that MSI-X remapping capped floods at 50/ms. A rate-limited flood is not the same thing as no interrupt delivery. Keep the numerical cap visible rather than replacing it with “eliminated.”
Does the cap tell us what happened to MSI-X interrupts already queued when a replacement driver started?

Not by itself. Limiting the flood rate and draining or rejecting already queued interrupts are different properties. This evidence reports the 50/ms remapping cap, but it does not separately report how many pending MSI-X interrupts were drained or whether any old interrupt reached the replacement.
The extension set out to verify interrupt drainage. Should I list drainage as verified in this result?

No. The reported interrupt finding is the MSI-X remapping cap of 50/ms. The activity’s intention to verify drainage does not supply a drainage outcome. If you report this evidence, distinguish the observed rate limit from any separate claim about queued-interrupt disposition.
What does ≤0.96 ms say about the unaffected devices?

It reports that unaffected-device response was no greater than 0.96 ms for the stated evidence. That is below the 1 ms service deadline. The ≤ sign describes an upper bound, not a claim that each response took exactly 0.96 ms.
How much below 1 ms is that?

The numerical difference is 0.04 ms: 1.00 ms minus 0.96 ms. It is a comparison between the reported response bound and the deadline, not a separately stated interrupt-handling budget or recovery-slot allocation.
May I say that the 50/ms interrupt cap caused the ≤0.96 ms response?

The evidence reports both findings, but does not isolate a causal contribution from the cap to the response bound. State that MSI-X remapping capped floods at 50/ms and that unaffected-device response was ≤0.96 ms. Do not attribute the entire timing result to remapping without a separate argument.
Does rejecting stale completions itself establish the 1 ms result?

No. Rejection is a restart-boundary correctness result; the ≤0.96 ms response is the timing result. Rejecting an old completion might require work, and the evidence does not quantify that work separately. The reported response bound addresses unaffected-device timing without making completion rejection and response time the same measurement.
Can I call the ≤0.96 ms figure the time it took to restart a driver?

No. It is an unaffected-device response bound. The evidence gives no time to complete a driver restart. The fact that it was reported across an extension involving 100 restarts does not turn service response into restart duration.
Does this establish the 1 ms admission certificate for every possible device?

It does not identify the subjects of individual admission certificates or state a new certificate-verification outcome. What this evidence directly reports is unaffected-device response ≤0.96 ms, together with the completion-rejection count and interrupt-rate cap. The response is below 1 ms at its reported scope, but it should not be turned into a universal certificate for every device or configuration.
Could I report zero stale completions accepted?

The explicit finding is that generation checks rejected 12,000 stale completions. It does not provide a separate accepted-stale-completion count. Describing the 12,000 as rejected is precise; reporting a global count of zero accepted would require an additional stated result or an exhaustive accounting of the completions at issue.
What about DMA isolation—does this provide a new no-escape finding?

No. This evidence is about generation checks on stale completions, MSI-X flood limiting, and unaffected-device response. It does not give a DMA-escape count, a cross-domain-write finding, or a peer-to-peer routing result. Those isolation properties should not be inferred from the reported timing and handoff results.
Should I say these figures hold under all repeated crashes and concurrent recoveries?

Do not extend the findings beyond the reported scope. The count covers 100 restarts, and the evidence reports the MSI-X flood cap and unaffected-device response alongside that result. It does not specify every crash pattern or concurrency arrangement to which the figures apply. A broader claim would need its own stated coverage.
If I need one sentence that preserves all three values without claiming a drainage result, what should it say?

Across 100 restarts, generation checks rejected 12,000 stale completions, MSI-X remapping capped floods at 50/ms, and unaffected-device response was ≤0.96 ms, below the 1 ms service deadline; no separate interrupt-drainage outcome is reported in these findings.
Let's adopt generation-tagged completions and a 50/ms MSI-X limit. BusGuard-1k kept unaffected-device response at ≤0.96 ms across 100 restarts. How should I state the decision?

State the adopted controls and the supporting timing result separately: adopt generation-tagged completions and limit MSI-X activity to 50 per millisecond. Across 100 restarts, BusGuard-1k kept unaffected-device response at ≤0.96 ms, below the 1 ms service deadline. The result supports the decision at its reported scope; it should not be presented as a guarantee for every possible restart condition.
What does adopting generation-tagged completions commit us to?

It makes driver generation part of how completions are distinguished across a crash and replacement. A completion associated with an earlier driver instance must not be mistaken for work belonging to the replacement merely because it arrives later.

The decision names generation-tagged completions, but it does not specify a tag format, a queue design, or a complete acceptance protocol.
Does that mean every kind of message and device event now has a generation tag?

No. The decision specifically adopts generation-tagged *completions*. It does not say that MSI-X interrupts, DMA transactions, or every other message carries the same tag. The 50/ms MSI-X limit is a separate control.
Should I describe the MSI-X limit as 50 interrupts total across the 100 restarts?

No. The unit is 50 per millisecond. The 100 figure counts restarts in the BusGuard-1k result; it is not the interval over which the MSI-X limit is expressed. Keep the rate and the restart count distinct.
Does a 50/ms limit mean exactly 50 interrupts are delivered every millisecond?
No. A limit constrains the rate; it does not require activity to reach that rate. The decision also does not give a total MSI-X interrupt count across the restarts.
Can I say the MSI-X limit rejects all interrupts left over from a crashed driver?

Not from this decision. Rate limiting MSI-X activity and deciding what happens to already queued interrupts are different properties. The decision adopts the 50/ms limit, but does not state a separate rule or result for rejecting every pending interrupt associated with an earlier driver instance.
Are generation-tagged completions meant to solve the MSI-X side as well?

They should remain separate in the wording. Generation tags distinguish completions by driver instance; the 50/ms limit constrains MSI-X activity. The decision does not say an MSI-X interrupt carries a completion tag or that limiting its rate determines whether it belongs to the replacement driver.
How strong is the unaffected-device timing finding?

BusGuard-1k reports unaffected-device response of no more than 0.96 ms across 100 restarts. That is below the 1 ms deadline by 0.04 ms. It is a positive result for the reported restarts, while the number of restarts limits the scope of what is explicitly reported.
Is 0.96 ms an average response time?
No. The result is expressed as ≤0.96 ms. Describe it as a response bound for unaffected devices across the reported 100 restarts, not as an average or as the exact duration of every response.
Does the 0.04 ms difference become an interrupt budget?

No. It is the arithmetic difference between the 1 ms service deadline and the ≤0.96 ms response bound. The decision does not allocate that difference specifically to MSI-X handling, completion checks, or any other work.
Could I say the replacement driver starts within 0.96 ms?
No. The ≤0.96 ms figure describes *unaffected-device response*, not the time needed to restart a driver. The decision gives no restart-completion bound.
Does BusGuard-1k prove that the 50/ms limit alone produced the response bound?

The decision reports both the adopted controls and the BusGuard-1k timing result, but it does not isolate the MSI-X limit's individual contribution to that result. Likewise, it does not attribute the whole response bound to generation-tagged completions. Keep the result tied to the reported run rather than assigning it to one control alone.
What if someone asks whether the decision covers DMA escapes or arbitrary driver writes?

Those remain distinct containment concerns for the overall driver boundary. This decision adopts completion tagging and an MSI-X rate limit and reports unaffected-device response across 100 restarts. It does not state a DMA-escape result or a cross-domain-write result as part of this decision.
Does adopting the controls mean they were only ideas under consideration?

No. “Adopt” is the decision here: generation-tagged completions and the 50/ms MSI-X limit are the chosen controls. That status is distinct from how broadly the BusGuard-1k result can be generalized. A choice can be definite while its reported timing evidence remains scoped to 100 restarts.
Should I call the 100 restarts 100 different fault scenarios?
No. The decision states the number of restarts, not a number of distinct scenarios. It does not give a breakdown of faults or say that each restart represented a different condition.
Does the reported bound guarantee a 1 ms deadline for the device whose driver crashes?
No. The result concerns unaffected devices. It does not assign a 1 ms response or restart deadline to the device whose driver crashes.
Can I say unaffected devices met the 1 ms requirement across the reported restarts?

Yes, if you preserve the precise reported result: their response stayed at ≤0.96 ms across 100 restarts, which is within 1 ms. Avoid extending that statement to all possible crashes, devices, or future restarts without further evidence.
What would be misleading about writing only, “Adopt rate-limited interrupts because recovery is safe”?

It omits generation-tagged completions, the specific 50/ms MSI-X limit, the ≤0.96 ms unaffected-device response bound, and the 100-restart scope. “Recovery is safe” also merges completion handling, interrupt behavior, timing, and other containment properties into a broader judgment than this decision states.
I want a short statement that keeps the decision and its evidence in one place without turning it into a universal guarantee.

Adopt generation-tagged completions and a 50/ms MSI-X limit. BusGuard-1k kept unaffected-device response at ≤0.96 ms across 100 restarts, within the 1 ms service deadline for those reported conditions.

I propose partitioning critical devices onto dedicated PCIe root complexes and IRQ cores, with reserved DRAM bandwidth and independent reset paths. How would that help the restartable driver boundary?

It separates several resources through which one device’s fault or recovery could interfere with another’s service. Dedicated PCIe root complexes address placement in the PCIe fabric; dedicated IRQ cores address where interrupt work runs; reserved DRAM bandwidth addresses memory-service contention; and independent reset paths address whether recovery of one device requires resetting a path used by another.

The proposal is directed at keeping unaffected critical devices serviceable during driver faults and concurrent recovery. The partitioning itself is not yet a verification that their 1 ms service deadlines hold.
Why does this proposal name four kinds of separation instead of just putting the drivers in separate address spaces?

An address-space boundary concerns memory access by driver code. It does not, by itself, separate PCIe routing, interrupt-processing capacity, DRAM service, or the effects of a reset. This proposal focuses on those additional sources of interference so a restart can be contained without relying on memory isolation alone to protect unaffected devices’ timing.

It does not replace the need to contain arbitrary driver writes and DMA; it proposes a hardware and service partition around critical devices.
What does it mean for a PCIe root complex to be dedicated in this context?

The proposal is to place critical devices on PCIe root complexes dedicated to their critical-device partition, rather than leaving the placement unspecified. That gives the isolation argument a defined PCIe boundary to examine when another device faults or restarts.

It does not specify how many root complexes exist, how many critical devices share one, or whether dedication alone prevents every possible DMA or timing effect.
Should I say each critical device has its own root complex?

No. The proposal says to partition critical devices onto dedicated PCIe root complexes; it does not require a one-to-one device-to-root-complex mapping. You can preserve the dedicated-placement requirement without adding a count or a particular grouping.
Does using a dedicated root complex automatically prove that peer-to-peer DMA cannot escape its IOMMU domain?

No. Placement on a dedicated root complex and enforcement of DMA isolation are distinct claims. The proposal can reduce the sharing that an isolation argument must consider, but it does not specify routing controls, requester-ID behavior, or an observed no-bypass result. DMA containment still needs to be established for the actual paths and domains.
Why give critical devices dedicated IRQ cores as well?

Interrupt handling can consume CPU service even when DMA remains confined. Dedicated IRQ cores are proposed to keep interrupt work for critical devices from being displaced by unrelated fault or recovery activity on a shared interrupt-processing core.

The proposal does not specify core counts, an interrupt rate, or an execution-time bound. Dedication gives a basis for protecting service; it is not, by itself, proof that every interrupt storm leaves the 1 ms deadlines intact.
Does a dedicated IRQ core mean the device has exclusive use of an entire CPU?

That is more specific than the proposal states. It calls for dedicated IRQ cores, not a complete description of everything that can execute on each core or an exclusive CPU allocation per device. The important proposed property is protected placement for interrupt work associated with critical-device service.
Could an interrupt flood still matter if the critical device has a dedicated IRQ core?

Yes. A core being dedicated does not automatically bound the amount of interrupt work directed to it or settle effects on other shared resources. The proposal must still coexist with containment of interrupt storms and verification of unaffected devices’ 1 ms deadlines. Dedicated placement should not be restated as a measured flood-handling result.
What is the distinction between reserved DRAM bandwidth and dedicated IRQ cores?

They protect different service resources. IRQ cores concern CPU capacity for interrupt work. Reserved DRAM bandwidth concerns access to memory service, which can be pressured by activity even if CPU placement is separate. Protecting one does not automatically protect the other.

The proposal names both so the timing argument for critical devices does not depend on a single resource boundary.
Does reserved DRAM bandwidth mean DMA from another device cannot reach critical-device memory?

No. A bandwidth reservation concerns timely access to DRAM, not which memory addresses DMA is permitted to write. DMA access restrictions require their own isolation boundary. Conversely, preventing an unauthorized DMA write does not establish that sufficient DRAM bandwidth remains available for a critical device’s service.
Is the reserved DRAM bandwidth a specified percentage?

No percentage or bandwidth amount is given. The proposal states that DRAM bandwidth is reserved, but does not specify the reservation’s size, allocation method, or verified worst-case service. Those details would matter to a concrete timing argument; they are not supplied here.
What is an independent reset path intended to protect?

It is intended to let a device-associated recovery use its reset path without making the reset path for an unaffected critical device depend on that recovery. That is relevant when crashes and restarts occur while other devices must keep receiving service.

The proposal does not describe the reset circuitry or prove that a reset produces no effects elsewhere. “Independent” is the proposed property to establish, not a reported measurement.
Would an independent reset path guarantee that restarting one driver cannot delay another device?

Not by itself. It addresses reset coupling, but interrupt processing, PCIe activity, and DRAM service can also affect timely operation. That is why the proposal includes all four elements. Whether the complete partition preserves unaffected devices’ 1 ms deadlines during faults and concurrent recovery remains a separate verification question.
Can we call the reset paths independent even if a reset of one device forces all critical devices to reset?

That would not express the independence this proposal needs. The point is to avoid making an unaffected critical device’s reset behavior contingent on recovery of another device. The proposal does not specify a concrete reset topology, so we should state the intended separation without claiming it has already been achieved.
What exactly is meant by “critical devices” here?

It identifies the devices to receive the proposed dedicated placement and reserved resources. In the overall design, the relevant hard-real-time condition is that unaffected devices retain verified 1 ms service deadlines during driver faults and concurrent recovery. The proposal does not list devices, establish how many are critical, or provide a classification procedure.
Does the proposal give the faulty device the same 1 ms deadline while it is being restarted?

No. The 1 ms service guarantee being protected is for unaffected devices. Partitioning critical devices does not create a stated 1 ms service or restart-completion deadline for a device whose own driver has crashed.
Would dedicated root complexes make all recovery work independent?

That would be too broad. A root-complex partition addresses one part of the hardware placement. The proposal separately names IRQ cores, DRAM bandwidth, and reset paths because recovery can interact with service through more than one resource. It gives no general finding that all recovery work is independent.
How should I think about the four elements together rather than treating each as a complete solution?

Treat them as complementary boundaries around critical-device service. PCIe placement addresses fabric sharing; IRQ-core placement addresses interrupt-processing sharing; DRAM reservation addresses memory-service contention; and reset-path independence addresses recovery coupling. Each can help bound a different way a fault or restart might affect an otherwise unaffected device.

The proposal succeeds as an assurance argument only if their combined behavior supports the deadline and containment requirements. Naming the boundaries alone does not establish that combined result.
If DRAM bandwidth is reserved, can I omit a check for interference from concurrent recovery?

No. A reservation is relevant to that check, but the proposal gives no numerical amount or finding about how recovery behaves while other devices need service. The requirement concerns the overlap: unaffected devices must retain their verified 1 ms deadlines during driver faults and concurrent recovery. That condition should not be assumed merely from the existence of a reservation.
Does this partition remove the need for restart fencing or for containing arbitrary driver writes?

No. Physical placement and reserved service do not, by themselves, constrain arbitrary driver memory writes or establish that stale DMA is fenced across a crash and restart. This proposal adds resource and reset separation for critical devices; it should not be presented as a substitute for the fault-containment properties of the restartable boundary.
What if the four proposed separations protect timing but DMA still reaches an unintended domain?

Then the overall containment goal would remain unmet. Preserving service and containing memory effects are distinct requirements that have to hold together. A timing-oriented partition cannot make an unintended DMA write acceptable, just as strong DMA isolation cannot excuse a missed 1 ms deadline for an unaffected device.
Conversely, what if all DMA is confined but a shared reset delays critical-device service?

That would leave the real-time side of the goal unanswered. The proposal includes independent reset paths precisely so recovery of one device is not simply assumed harmless to another’s service. But without a verified timing result, we should describe that as the intended protection, not as a conclusion about any particular reset.
Is it appropriate to say the partition guarantees there will be no shared bottleneck anywhere?

No. The proposal names specific resources to partition or reserve; it does not enumerate every possible shared resource or show that every source of interference is eliminated. Its concrete claim at this stage is the proposed arrangement: dedicated PCIe root complexes and IRQ cores, reserved DRAM bandwidth, and independent reset paths for critical devices.
Could the critical devices share a dedicated IRQ core with each other?

The proposal does not specify the mapping of devices to cores. “Dedicated IRQ cores” identifies protected cores for critical-device interrupt work but supplies neither a one-core-per-device rule nor a claim that multiple critical devices share a core. A specific mapping and its deadline effects would require additional information.
Should I describe the reserved DRAM bandwidth as a recovery budget?

Not automatically. The proposal says critical devices have reserved DRAM bandwidth. It does not identify that reservation as bandwidth assigned to recovery or specify how recovery uses memory. Calling it a recovery budget could reverse the purpose of the reservation without support.
What would have to be verified before calling this a hard-real-time partition?

The relevant check is whether unaffected critical devices retain their 1 ms service deadlines while driver faults and concurrent recovery exercise the proposed PCIe, IRQ, DRAM, and reset boundaries. The DMA and arbitrary-write containment requirements also remain relevant to the complete driver boundary.

This proposal provides no device placement, bandwidth quantity, reset trace, or deadline result. It identifies an arrangement to evaluate rather than a completed verification.
Can you give me a compact statement of the proposal without implying it is already implemented?

Propose partitioning critical devices onto dedicated PCIe root complexes and IRQ cores, reserving DRAM bandwidth for their service, and providing independent reset paths. The intended effect is to contain recovery interference so unaffected devices can retain verified 1 ms service deadlines during faults and concurrent recovery; implementation and verification are not stated here.

I want to deploy partitioned PCIe root complexes with the adopted generation checks and MSI-X limits, then verify independent resets, DMA containment, and unaffected devices’ 1 ms service deadlines. How should I frame that plan?

Frame deployment and verification as separate planned steps. Deploy the partitioned root complexes together with the adopted generation checks and MSI-X limits. Then verify that resets are independent, DMA remains contained, and unaffected devices retain their 1 ms service deadlines during driver faults and concurrent recovery.

The plan does not say deployment has finished or that any of those three verification checks has passed.
What exactly does “partitioned root complexes” commit us to in this plan?

It commits the planned deployment to a PCIe root-complex partition rather than leaving the critical-device placement on a shared, unspecified fabric. It does not give a root-complex count, a device-to-complex mapping, or a finding that the partition is independently resettable or DMA-isolated. Those latter properties are among the things to verify.
Does this plan say every critical device gets its own root complex?
No. It calls for partitioned root complexes without specifying a one-to-one mapping. Saying each critical device has its own would add a placement rule the plan does not contain.
When I mention the adopted generation checks, can I identify them as checks on completions?

Yes. The adopted generation mechanism concerns completions associated with driver instances. In this deployment plan, those checks should remain part of the restart boundary so work associated with a crashed instance is not simply treated as the replacement’s work. The plan does not specify the checks’ implementation details or report a new handoff result from the deployed partition.
And can I state the numerical MSI-X limit?

The adopted limit is 50 MSI-X interrupts per millisecond, or 50/ms. You can name it to make “MSI-X limits” precise. That is an interrupt-rate limit, not a 50 ms restart limit or a statement that exactly 50 interrupts arrive in each millisecond.
Do the generation checks and the MSI-X limit perform the same job?

No. Generation checks distinguish completions associated with different driver instances. The MSI-X limit constrains interrupt activity. Both matter around a crash and restart, but a completion check does not rate-limit interrupts, and an interrupt-rate limit does not identify a completion’s generation.
Does saying the controls are adopted mean this deployment has already been validated?

No. “Adopted” identifies the controls selected for the plan. Deploying them with partitioned root complexes and verifying the combined arrangement are still the work described here. The adoption decision should not be converted into a new result for the planned deployment.
Why do independent resets need their own verification if the root complexes are partitioned?

Partitioning the PCIe placement does not, by itself, establish how reset paths behave. The verification must determine whether a reset associated with one partition can be carried out without resetting or otherwise coupling the service of an unaffected partition. Independent resets are an explicit check rather than an automatic consequence of the word “partitioned.”

The plan gives no reset topology or observed reset behavior.
Is that verification a check that every reset completes within 1 ms?

No. The 1 ms figure is the service deadline for unaffected devices, not a reset-completion deadline. Verifying reset independence and verifying the 1 ms service deadlines are related but distinct checks: a reset’s effect on another device’s service matters even though its own completion time is not assigned a 1 ms limit here.
What would be too strong a claim about independent resets at this stage?

Saying that resets cannot affect any other device would be too strong before the check is performed, and it would be broader than the stated verification target. The plan is to verify independence in the deployed arrangement; it provides no result about a particular reset or every possible shared effect.
What does the DMA-containment check need to keep separate from the reset check?

It needs to address whether device-initiated memory activity remains within its intended isolation boundary, including across fault and restart. Reset independence asks whether recovering one partition disrupts another through the reset path. A reset can be independent without proving that DMA is contained, and DMA can be contained without proving that resets are independent.

The plan calls for verification of both rather than using one as evidence for the other.
Can I infer DMA containment from dedicated root-complex placement alone?

No. Placement may make paths easier to distinguish, but it does not by itself establish which DMA transactions are permitted or where they are enforced. The plan explicitly includes DMA-containment verification, so a no-escape result cannot be assumed from the partition’s proposed layout.
Does a 50/ms MSI-X limit establish DMA containment?

No. MSI-X limiting concerns interrupt delivery. It does not constrain the addresses or routing of device-initiated DMA. The limit is part of the planned deployment, while DMA containment remains a separate property to verify.
Is the 1 ms verification only about normal operation after deployment?

No. The underlying service requirement concerns unaffected devices during driver faults and concurrent recovery. A check made only when no fault or recovery is occurring would not establish that condition for the deployed boundary. The plan’s deadline verification should be read against that fault-and-recovery requirement.
Should we count the restarting device as one of the unaffected devices in that check?

No. The stated 1 ms guarantee is for devices unaffected by the driver fault. The plan does not promise that a device whose own driver is restarting continues to receive service within 1 ms or that its restart finishes within 1 ms.
Could independent resets and DMA containment both verify successfully while the 1 ms check fails?

Conceptually, yes. Those first two checks address reset coupling and memory-access containment; neither alone bounds all timing interference during fault handling and concurrent recovery.
